extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and illustrative case examples for evaluating patent claim language under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (¶¶1, 2, and 6), including when terms are definite or indefinite, when means-plus-function treatment is invoked, and related written-description/enablement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional terms in claims (e.g., 'spongy', 'porous', 'transparent to infrared rays', 'fragile gel') must be examined to determine whether they provide sufficient particularity and distinctness under § 112, ¶2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language can be indefinite when it defines a claim only by what it does rather than what it is (United Carbon; Halliburton). Courts look to the intrinsic record (specification, figures, prosecution history) to find objective meaning or standards; if the intrinsic evidence provides a guideline or examples so a person of ordinary skill can determine scope, the term may be definite (In re Swinehart; Enzo Biochem). If the term leaves unresolved how to measure the required degree of a functional property (e.g., how 'fragile' a gel must be), it is indefinite (Halliburton). See MPEP 2173.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative terminology: terms of degree and subjective terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of degree and apparently subjective descriptors (e.g., 'essentially free of', 'substantially equal to', 'so dimensioned', 'substantial absence of slug flow', 'aesthetically pleasing', 'readily installed') raise definiteness issues under § 112, ¶2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such terms are not automatically indefinite. The court evaluates whether the specification supplies a standard or examples that enable a person of ordinary skill to measure the claimed degree (In re Marosi; Seattle Box; Orthokinetics; Exxon; Hearing Components). Purely subjective terms lacking an objective anchor (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing' without a workable objective standard) are indefinite (Datamize). Where the specification, figures, or intrinsic evidence provide a standard (e.g., 'requires no tools', figures showing examples, relationship to reactor efficiency), the term may be definite (Hearing Components; Young v. Lumenis; Exxon). See MPEP 2173.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical ranges and measurement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting numerical ranges or amounts must be interpretable by a person of ordinary skill in light of the specification and must not leave ambiguity as to how the numbers are measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different accepted sample-preparation or measurement methods produce materially different values (so that the claimed numerical limitation could vary depending on method), the intrinsic record must specify or at least clearly point to acceptable measurement methods. Failure to specify acceptable measurement/sample-preparation methods when necessary can render a claim indefinite (Honeywell v. ITC). See MPEP 2173.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms must have proper antecedent basis so that references like 'said' or 'the' refer to a clearly identified previously recited element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous antecedent usage can cause indefiniteness; small wording changes (e.g., 'at the separation' → 'at a separation') may resolve the problem. The specification context is consulted to determine whether a person skilled in the art would understand the antecedent (In re Skvorecz). See MPEP 2173.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of art and industry-specific terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms of art (e.g., 'POL regulator') are evaluated for definiteness based on whether intrinsic evidence and the knowledge of one skilled in the art give them a clear meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the intrinsic record shows that the term is well known and its locations/functions are understood by a POSITA, the term is not indefinite (Power-One). Examiners/ courts will construe such terms in view of the specification and the ordinary meaning in the art. See MPEP 2173.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth alone does not equal indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is broad in scope is not automatically indefinite under § 112, ¶2 provided it sufficiently notifies the public of the claim's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to broad genera or formulae with many possible combinations can be definite if the intrinsic evidence enables the public to determine whether a given embodiment falls within the claims (Ultimax Cement). The standard is whether the claim sufficiently notifies the public of the patentee's right to exclude. See MPEP 2173.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between specification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be read in the context of the specification; claims that are inconsistent with the specification's definitions or examples can be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim cannot be read apart from and independent of the disclosure on which it is based. If the claim language is inherently inconsistent with the written description (e.g., claims call for an outcome the specification indicates is not produced by the recited steps or materials), the claims are indefinite (In re Cohn). See MPEP 2173.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether non-structural claim terms invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶6 (means-plus-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations expressed using terms other than 'means for' (e.g., 'mechanism', 'member', 'element', 'circuit', 'detector', 'assembly') may nonetheless be treated as means-plus-function under § 112, ¶6 if they do not recite sufficient structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis considers whether the term connotes sufficiently definite structure to one skilled in the art. If not, the limitation may be interpreted under ¶6 and limited to the corresponding structure disclosed in the specification and equivalents. The 2011 Supplementary Guidelines provide factors and case examples to determine when these alternative terms invoke ¶6. See Section II and MPEP § 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'mechanism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the term 'mechanism' in a claim can invoke means-plus-function treatment when the claim fails to recite structure for performing the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether 'mechanism' in context connotes sufficient structure. If not, the claim limitation may be governed by § 112, ¶6 and limited to the structures disclosed for performing the function (Greenberg v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery and related examples in Section II.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'member'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'member' can be non-structural and trigger § 112, ¶6 analysis if it is used generically without structural detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether 'member' as used connotes structure or is merely a nonce word substituting for 'means.' If the latter, treat as means-plus-function and apply ¶6 analysis (examples provided in Section II.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'element'
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting an 'element' may invoke means-plus-function analysis when the 'element' is defined only by function and lacks structural definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the term 'element' in context imparts sufficient structure. If not, limit the claim to the disclosed structure that performs the function under § 112, ¶6 (Section II.C examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'circuit' / 'circuitry'
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms such as 'circuit' or 'circuitry' may or may not connote sufficient structure; when used generically they can trigger ¶6 treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'circuit' is accompanied by structural language (e.g., electronic components, interconnections) it may avoid ¶6. If merely functional and lacking structural detail, treat under ¶6 and confine to corresponding structures disclosed (Section II.D examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'detector'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'detector' recited without structural detail may be treated under means-plus-function rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the 'detector' term in context conveys sufficiently definite structure; if not, limit to the corresponding structure in the specification and equivalents (Section II.E examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific non-means terms that may invoke ¶6: 'assembly'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'assembly' can be a generic placeholder; if it lacks structural definition it may invoke § 112, ¶6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether 'assembly' is presented with structural detail; absent such detail, constrain the claim to disclosed structure performing the function (Section II.F examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of §112, ¶6 (means-plus-function) and §112, ¶2 (indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claim limitations may both invoke ¶6 (as means-plus-function) and raise indefiniteness concerns under ¶2; examiners must evaluate both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guidelines use case examples to show when a limitation should be treated under ¶6 and then evaluated for definiteness under ¶2 (III.A: examples where indefiniteness rejection is appropriate) and when treatment under ¶6 does not render the claim indefinite (III.B: examples where rejection not appropriate). Consider whether an objective standard or disclosed corresponding structure resolves any vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement for claimed scope (§112, ¶1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be enabled across their full scope; if a claim is broad enough to cover multiple embodiments (e.g., video games and movies), the specification must enable the full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that covers multiple distinct embodiments must enable each embodiment; lacking enabling disclosure for a claimed embodiment (e.g., how to integrate user images into movies) may render the claim invalid for lack of enablement (Atari v. North American Philips; example in Section IV.B and '825 patent analysis). See doctrine discussed in Section IV.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description support for claims limited to a subset of disclosed problems/solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim that addresses only one of several problems disclosed (or only one of several disclosed solutions) is supported by the written description under §112, ¶1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that discloses multiple problems and multiple solutions need not have every claim address every disclosed problem/solution. A claim limited to one disclosed solution or one problem is supported if the specification conveys possession of the invention recited in that claim (Revolution Eyewear; Crown Packaging). The key is whether the disclosure shows the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-means-type claims and the enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims drafted as a single means-plus-function limitation without reciting a combination (a 'single means' claim) raise enablement and §112 issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'single-means' claim (a claim whose body is only a means-plus-function limitation and additional language merely describes the means) does not satisfy §112, ¶1 because it would embrace all conceivable structures for performing the function while the specification discloses only specific structures. Such claims are subject to rejection for lack of enablement (In re Hyatt; discussion in MPEP §§ 2164.08(a), 2181 V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intrinsic evidence (specification, dependent claims, prosecution history) as objective anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence can supply objective standards or examples that make otherwise vague claim language definite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts rely on dependent claims, specification examples, declared suitable structures, figures, and prosecution statements to construe terms lacking numerical precision (Enzo Biochem—dependent claim specified a particular linkage group; specification provided suitable examples and measurement techniques such as thermal denaturation profiles). Examiners should look to these intrinsic sources before finding indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble, prosecution history, and claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble language and statements made during prosecution may limit or clarify claim scope and affect definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements distinguishing prior art or characterizing the invention during prosecution (or limiting language in the preamble) can render ambiguous terms definite by showing the applicant's intended meaning (Halliburton: preamble and prosecution distinguished 'fragile gel' to limit scope). Consider prosecution history and claim context when construing terms.
